A '''judgment sample''', also known as an '''expert''' or '''purposive''' sample, is a type of non-random [[sample (statistics)|sample]], where a researcher or expert selects the sample based on who they believe would be most useful or appropriate for the study.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Ahmed |first=Sirwan Khalid |date=December 2024 |title=How to choose a sampling technique and determine sample size for research: A simplified guide for researchers |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S2772906024005089 |journal=Oral Oncology Reports |language=en |volume=12 |article-number=100662 |doi=10.1016/j.oor.2024.100662}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Deming |first=W. Edwards |title=Sample Design in business research |publisher=John Wiley and Sons |year=1990 |isbn=0-471-52370-4 |page=31}}</ref> 

Results obtained from a judgment sample are subject to some degree of [[Sampling bias|bias]] and may be hard to [[External validity#In experiments|generalize]], due to the chosen sample not representing the larger population.<ref name=":0" /> 

A random sample would provide less bias, but potentially less raw information.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Palinkas |first=Lawrence A. |last2=Horwitz |first2=Sarah M. |last3=Green |first3=Carla A. |last4=Wisdom |first4=Jennifer P. |last5=Duan |first5=Naihua |last6=Hoagwood |first6=Kimberly |date=September 2015 |title=Purposeful Sampling for Qualitative Data Collection and Analysis in Mixed Method Implementation Research |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s10488-013-0528-y |journal=Administration and Policy in Mental Health and Mental Health Services Research |language=en |volume=42 |issue=5 |pages=533–544 |doi=10.1007/s10488-013-0528-y |issn=0894-587X |pmc=4012002 |pmid=24193818}}</ref> The pitfalls of this system are significant because of bias, limited statistical methods, and limits to an expert's ability to choose a good sample.
